paragraphs.heading: What is in it
paragraphs.text: Seawater is water from a sea or an ocean. Its average salinity across the world's oceans is about 3.5%, which means each kilogram, roughly a litre, holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts. The most abundant dissolved ions are sodium, chloride, magnesium, sulfate and calcium.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same everywhere
paragraphs.text: Most seawater has a salinity between 31 and 38 g/kg, but it is not evenly salty around the world. Where it mixes with fresh water from river mouths, melting glaciers or very heavy rain, it can be much less salty. The saltiest open sea is the Red Sea, where evaporation is high, rain and river inflow are low, and circulation is confined. Isolated bodies of water can be considerably saltier again: in the Dead Sea salinity is about ten times higher.

paragraphs.heading: Heavier and harder to freeze
paragraphs.text: Seawater is denser than fresh water and pure water, because the dissolved salts add proportionally more mass than volume. At the surface its density runs from about 1020 to 1029 kg/m³, depending on temperature and salinity. Deep down, under high pressure, it can reach 1050 kg/m³ or more. Salt also lowers the freezing point, and the more salt, the lower it goes. The coldest liquid seawater on record turned up in 2010, in a stream beneath an Antarctic glacier, at −2.6 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Different from river water
paragraphs.text: Seawater holds more dissolved ions than any type of fresh water, but the proportions are very different. Take bicarbonate. Seawater has about 2.8 times more of it than river water does. Yet bicarbonate makes up 48% of what is dissolved in river water and only 0.14% of what is dissolved in seawater. Gaps like this come from differing residence times: sodium and chloride have very long ones, while calcium tends to precipitate much sooner.

paragraphs.heading: The pH of seawater
paragraphs.text: The pH of seawater usually stays between 7.5 and 8.4. In deep ocean water it is naturally lower, down to 7.8, a result of organic matter breaking down there, and it can reach 8.4 in surface water where biological productivity is high. Measuring it is not simple. The chemistry of seawater complicates the job, several different pH scales are in use, and readings on different scales may differ by up to 0.14 units. Between 1950 and 2020 the average pH at the ocean surface dropped from about 8.15 to 8.05.

paragraphs.heading: Life in a litre
paragraphs.text: In 1957 researchers from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography sampled Pacific water and counted bacteria two ways: directly under the microscope, and by growing cultures. In some cases the direct counts were up to 10 000 times the culture counts. The gap was put down to bacteria clumped in aggregates, to culture media that favour some kinds, and to inactive cells. In the 1990s, better techniques that probe small snippets of DNA let researchers in the Census of Marine Life identify thousands of microbes nobody had known. One litre of seawater may contain over 20,000 species.
